How to use this primer

This booklet teaches thermo-fluid devices from zero, in the order the exam needs it. Read it once before the Complete Solutions. Each section has a green core idea box (learn this first), the formulas with every symbol and unit, a key figure and a short worked example. Section 2 is a maths and units refresher: most marks lost in this course come from unit slips (mm vs m, °C vs K, L/min vs m3/s) and from using the wrong k or R for a gas.

The pass set (from the Question Map): pipe flow (A1, A2), flow meters (A4), centrifugal pumps (A5-A7), reciprocating pumps (A8), compressible flow and nozzles (B1, B2) and heat exchangers (B4-B6). The question numbers move between years (in 2019 and 2023 whole topics changed sections), so learn by topic. Dimensional analysis (A3), compressors and fans (A9) and shocks (B3) are the next to add.

The whole course on one page

Read the map in three blocks: moving liquids through pipes (losses) and measuring how much flows; machines that give the fluid energy (pumps, fans, compressors); and hot and fast gases: compressible flow in nozzles, then heat exchangers that pass heat from one fluid to another.

Maths and units refresher

Convert everything to SI before you start: m, kg, s, N, Pa, W, K. Write the unit on every line. Keep 4 significant figures until the boxed answer.

Conversions you will meet

QuantityConversion
flow rate1 L/s = 10−3 m3/s; 1 L/min = 1.667×10−5 m3/s; 1 gpm (US) = 6.309×10−5 m3/s
pressure1 bar = 105 Pa; 1 atm = 101.325 kPa; 1 m of water = 9.81 kPa; 1 mm Hg = 133.3 Pa
power1 hp = 746 W (0.746 kW); 1 kW = 1000 J/s
length1 in = 25.4 mm; 1 ft = 0.3048 m
temperatureT(K) = T(°C) + 273.15; a temperature difference is the same in K and °C
speedrpm → rad/s: ω = 2πN/60; blade speed u = πDN/60

Logarithms and exponentials

  • ln is the natural log (base e); ln(a/b) = ln a − ln b; ln(1) = 0; if ln x = y then x = ey.
  • LMTD (log mean temperature difference): (ΔT1 − ΔT2)/ln(ΔT1/ΔT2). Either order gives the same answer (top and bottom both change sign).
  • e−x falls from 1 towards 0: e−1 = 0.368, e−2 = 0.135, e−3 = 0.050.

Powers and roots

  • xaxb = xa+b, (xa)b = xab, x3/4 = (√√x)3.
  • Isentropic powers for air (k = 1.4): k/(k − 1) = 3.5, (k − 1)/k = 0.2857, 1/(k − 1) = 2.5, (k − 1)/2 = 0.2.
  • Gas constants: air R = 287 J/kg K, cp = 1005; CO2 R = 188.9, k = 1.289; helium R = 2077, k = 1.667.

Dimensions

Every quantity can be written in M (mass), L (length), T (time): velocity LT−1, force MLT−2, pressure ML−1T−2, density ML−3, viscosity μ ML−1T−1, power ML2T−3. A correct equation has the same dimensions in every term.

Fluid basics and Bernoulli’s equation

A flowing fluid carries three kinds of energy per unit weight (‘heads’, in metres): pressure head P/ρg, velocity head V2/2g and elevation z. With no friction and no machine their sum is constant along a streamline (Bernoulli). Friction removes head (hL); a pump adds head.

P1/ρg + V12/2g + z1 + hpump = P2/ρg + V22/2g + z2 + hL; Q = AV = constant

SymbolMeaningUnit
Pstatic pressurePa
ρdensity (water 1000)kg/m3
Vmean velocitym/s
zheight above datumm
hLhead loss (friction)m
Qvolume flow ratem3/s
μ, νdynamic viscosity, kinematic viscosity μ/ρPa s, m2/s

Flow in pipes (A1, A2)

The Reynolds number Re = ρVD/μ (inertia/viscous force) decides the type of flow: smooth layers (laminar, Re < 2300) or chaotic eddies (turbulent, Re > 4000). Friction head loss in a pipe is found by Darcy-Weisbach with a friction factor f: 64/Re if laminar, from the Moody chart if turbulent.

hL = f (L/D)(V2/2g); laminar f = 64/Re, ΔP = 32μLV/D2; minor loss hm = K V2/2g; pumping power W = QΔP

SymbolMeaningUnit
fDarcy friction factor–
L, Dpipe length and inside diameterm
ε/Drelative roughness–
Kloss coefficient of a fitting–
Lhentrance (hydrodynamic) lengthm

Example: water at 0.2 m/s in a 10 mm pipe, ν = 10−6: Re = 0.2 × 0.01/10−6 = 2000 (laminar), f = 0.032, over 10 m: hL = 0.032 × 1000 × 0.04/19.62 = 0.065 m.

Series and parallel pipes: in series the same Q passes and the losses add; in parallel each branch has the same loss and the flows add.

Dimensional analysis (A3)

If you know which variables a quantity depends on, you can group them into a few dimensionless numbers (π groups). This cuts the number of experiments and gives scale-model rules. Buckingham: n variables in m fundamental dimensions give n − m groups.

  1. List the variables and their dimensions (M, L, T).
  2. Choose m repeating variables that together contain M, L and T but do not form a group on their own (usually D, V, ρ).
  3. Form each π = DaVbρc×(one other variable); solve the powers so π is dimensionless.
  4. Write π1 = f(π2, π3, ...).

Example: drag F on a sphere depends on D, V, ρ, μ: n = 5, m = 3, 2 groups: F/(ρV2D2) = f(ρVD/μ) = f(Re).

Measuring flow (A4)

Most flow meters squeeze the flow (venturi, orifice, nozzle): velocity rises, pressure falls, and the measured pressure drop gives the velocity by Bernoulli. A Pitot tube instead stops the flow and reads the extra (stagnation) pressure. A rotameter and a turbine meter read flow directly from a float position or a rotor speed.

Q = Cd a1a2√(2gh) / √(a12 − a22); h = x(Sm/S − 1); Pitot V = Cv√(2gh)

SymbolMeaningUnit
a1, a2inlet and throat areasm2
Cdcoefficient of discharge (venturi 0.95-0.99, orifice about 0.62)–
hpressure difference as head of flowing fluidm
xmanometer readingm
Sm, Sspecific gravity of manometer liquid and of flowing liquid–

Example: mercury manometer reads x = 0.2 m on water: h = 0.2(13.6 − 1) = 2.52 m of water; a Pitot tube then gives V = √(2 × 9.81 × 2.52) = 7.03 m/s.

Centrifugal pumps (A5, A6, A7)

A rotating impeller throws the liquid outwards; the casing (volute or diffuser) turns its high speed into pressure. The head the pump gives depends on blade speed and outlet whirl velocity (H = Vw2u2/g ideally). Its performance at any speed follows the affinity laws, its type follows the specific speed, and it fails by cavitation if the suction pressure falls to the vapour pressure.

Work/weight = Vw2u2/g; ηmano = gHm/(Vw2u2); P = ρgQH/ηo; Ns = N√Q/H3/4; Q ∝ N, H ∝ N2, P ∝ N3

SymbolMeaningUnit
u2blade tip speed πD2N/60m/s
Vw2whirl (tangential) component of outlet velocitym/s
Hmmanometric headm
Nspeedrpm
Nsspecific speedrpm, m, m3/s
NPSH (net positive suction head)net positive suction headm

Example: a pump gives 20 m at 1450 rpm; at 1800 rpm: H = 20(1800/1450)2 = 30.8 m, and the flow rises by 1800/1450 = 1.24 times.

Reciprocating pumps, compressors and fans (A8, A9)

A reciprocating pump is a piston in a cylinder with suction and delivery valves: it moves a fixed volume per stroke, so it gives high pressure at low flow. The difference between the swept (theoretical) and actual delivery is the slip. Fans, blowers and compressors do for gases what pumps do for liquids; they are ranked by pressure ratio.

Qth = ALN/60 (single acting), 2ALN/60 (double acting); Cd = Qact/Qth; slip = Qth − Qact; P = ρgQth(hs + hd)

SymbolMeaningUnit
Apiston area πD2/4m2
Lstroke lengthm
Ncrank speedrpm
hs, hdsuction and delivery headsm

Example: D = 0.15 m, L = 0.3 m, 60 rpm single acting: Qth = 0.01767 × 0.3 × 1 = 5.30 L/s; if 5.0 L/s is delivered, Cd = 0.943 and slip = 5.7%.

Compressible flow and nozzles (B1, B2, B3)

When gas moves at a good fraction of the speed of sound, its density changes, and kinetic energy comes from its enthalpy: it cools as it speeds up. The Mach number Ma = V/c measures this. A subsonic flow speeds up in a converging duct, a supersonic flow in a diverging duct, so a rocket nozzle converges to a sonic throat and then diverges. Supersonic flow that must slow suddenly does it through a shock wave.

c = √(kRT); T0/T = 1 + (k − 1)Ma2/2; P0/P = (T0/T)k/(k−1); dA/A = (Ma2 − 1)dV/V; ṁ = ρAV

SymbolMeaningUnit
MaMach number V/c–
cspeed of soundm/s
kspecific heat ratio cp/cv (air 1.4)–
Rgas constant (air 287)J/kg K
T0, P0stagnation temperature and pressureK, Pa
*critical (sonic, Ma = 1) state–

Example: air from a tank at 500 K: at the throat T* = 0.8333 × 500 = 417 K and V* = √(1.4 × 287 × 417) = 409 m/s.

Heat exchangers (B4, B5, B6)

A heat exchanger passes heat from a hot fluid to a cold fluid through a wall. The rate is Q = UAΔTlm, where U collects all the resistances and ΔTlm is the proper average temperature difference. When outlet temperatures are unknown, use the effectiveness-NTU method instead. Counter flow always does better than parallel flow.

Q = ṁhcph(Th,i − Th,o) = ṁccpc(Tc,o − Tc,i) = UAΔTlm; ε = Q/[Cmin(Th,i − Tc,i)]; NTU (number of transfer units) = UA/Cmin

SymbolMeaningUnit
Uoverall heat transfer coefficientW/m2K
Aheat transfer area πDLm2
ΔTlmlog mean temperature differenceK or °C
Cheat capacity rate ṁcpW/K
CrCmin/Cmax–
Rffouling factorm2K/W

Example: water 0.5 kg/s heated 20 → 60 °C by oil 120 → 80 °C in counter flow, U = 300: Q = 0.5 × 4180 × 40 = 83.6 kW; ΔT1 = ΔT2 = 60 °C so ΔTlm = 60; A = 83,600/(300 × 60) = 4.64 m2.
